title: Kolmogorov–Arnold–Moser Theorem
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: In a nearly integrable Hamiltonian system, most invariant tori with sufficiently irrational frequencies survive small perturbations and form a Cantor set of positive measure.
latex: H(I,\theta)=h(I)+\varepsilon f(I,\theta) \Rightarrow \text{Cantor family of invariant tori}
short: Order survives small perturbations, but not everywhere.
long: Order survives small perturbations, but not everywhere. The surviving tori have Diophantine frequency vectors; resonant tori generally break.
proof: Iterate Newton-like coordinate transformations satisfying Diophantine nonresonance conditions, with measure estimates on the removed resonant sets.
consequence: It explains long-term stability in nearly integrable mechanical systems.

title: Sharkovsky Ordering of Periodic Points
subject: Differential Equations
statement: For a continuous map of an interval, existence of a period-m point forces periods that follow m in the Sharkovsky ordering; period three comes first and forces all periods.
short: One period forces a whole cascade of others in a surprising order.
long: One period forces a whole cascade of others in a surprising order. The ordering is a total order on the positive integers with 3 at the head and 1 at the tail.
proof: Analyse the interval images of a period-m orbit and construct periodic points via the intermediate value theorem.
consequence: It gives a sharp existence theory for periodic points of one-dimensional maps.

title: Euler Reflection Formula for the Gamma Function
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: For every complex z that is not an integer, the Gamma function satisfies a product identity with the sine function.
short: Gamma values at complementary arguments multiply to a trigonometric reciprocal.
long: Gamma values at complementary arguments multiply to a trigonometric reciprocal. It gives Gamma(1/2) = sqrt(pi) and controls the poles at nonpositive integers.
proof: Combine the Weierstrass product for Gamma with the Euler product for sine.
consequence: It evaluates many definite integrals and fixes analytic continuation normalisations.

title: Beta–Gamma Integral Identity
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: The beta integral equals a quotient of Gamma functions whenever the real parts of its parameters are positive.
short: A finite-interval integral is a ratio of Gamma functions.
long: A finite-interval integral is a ratio of Gamma functions. The same identity holds for the integral over the positive real line after the substitution t = u/(1+u).
proof: Write Gamma(a)Gamma(b) as a double integral over the positive quadrant and change variables to separate the beta integral.
consequence: It unifies probability normalising constants with special-function algebra.

title: Legendre Duplication Formula
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: The Gamma function satisfies a doubling relation linking Gamma(z), Gamma(z+1/2), and Gamma(2z).
short: Halving the argument introduces a power of two and sqrt(pi).
long: Halving the argument introduces a power of two and sqrt(pi). It is the case p=2 of the Gauss multiplication theorem.
proof: Apply the beta integral with a=b=z and the substitution t=(1+u)/2.
consequence: It simplifies normalisations of beta and chi-square distributions.

title: Stirling's Asymptotic Formula for n!
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: Factorials grow like sqrt(2 pi n)(n/e)^n, with a logarithmic expansion whose leading correction is of order 1/n.
short: Laplace's method turns the integral for n! into elementary asymptotics.
long: Laplace's method turns the integral for n! into elementary asymptotics. The full Stirling series is divergent but optimally truncatable.
proof: Apply Laplace's method to Gamma(n+1) = integral of x^n exp(-x) over x positive.
consequence: It is indispensable in combinatorics, statistics, and statistical mechanics.

title: Legendre Polynomial Orthogonality
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: Legendre polynomials are orthogonal on the interval from minus one to one with a normalisation depending on the degree.
short: Different angular momenta give independent modes.
long: Different angular momenta give independent modes. They arise as eigenfunctions of a singular Sturm–Liouville problem with weight one.
proof: Use Rodrigues' formula and integrate by parts n times; boundary terms vanish because (x^2-1)^n has n-fold zeros at the endpoints.
consequence: It enables spectral expansion of functions on the sphere with axial symmetry.

title: Three-Term Recurrence for Orthogonal Polynomials
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: Monic orthogonal polynomials for a positive measure satisfy a three-term recurrence whose subdiagonal coefficients are positive.
short: Orthogonality forces locality in the polynomial basis.
long: Orthogonality forces locality in the polynomial basis. The coefficients encode the moments of the underlying measure.
proof: Expand xP_n in the orthogonal basis; orthogonality kills all but three terms, and positivity of squared norms gives b_n>0.
consequence: It underlies stable evaluation and the Lanczos algorithm.

title: Christoffel–Darboux Identity
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: The reproducing kernel for orthogonal polynomials has a closed two-term form involving the last two polynomials and the ratio of leading coefficients.
short: A long sum collapses to a short determinantal formula.
long: A long sum collapses to a short determinantal formula. Here k_n denotes the leading coefficient of the n-th orthonormal polynomial.
proof: Apply the three-term recurrence at x and y, multiply crosswise, subtract, and telescope the sum.
consequence: It gives reproducing kernels, Christoffel numbers, and sharp kernel bounds.

title: Jacobi Elliptic Functions and Doubly Periodic Meromorphy
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: The Jacobi elliptic functions are doubly periodic meromorphic functions generalising sine and cosine, and the function sn satisfies a first-order algebraic differential equation.
short: Elliptic functions invert elliptic integrals.
long: Elliptic functions invert elliptic integrals. The modulus k controls the ratio of the two periods; limiting cases give ordinary trigonometric or hyperbolic functions.
proof: Invert the integral from zero to phi of dtheta/sqrt(1-k^2 sin^2 theta) and differentiate.
consequence: They parametrise pendulum motion and nonlinear wave profiles.

title: Euler–Maclaurin Summation Formula
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: A finite sum differs from the corresponding integral by endpoint correction terms involving Bernoulli numbers and derivatives of the summand.
short: Sums are integrals plus boundary corrections.
long: Sums are integrals plus boundary corrections. Optimally truncating the correction series often gives exponentially accurate approximations.
proof: Integrate by parts repeatedly using Bernoulli polynomials, whose derivatives differ by one.
consequence: It connects discrete and continuous analysis and supplies quadrature error expansions.

title: Poincaré Asymptotic Expansion Definition
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: A function has an asymptotic expansion relative to an asymptotic scale if the remainder after N terms is little-o of the N-th scale function as the limit is approached.
short: Asymptotic series describe limiting behaviour without needing convergence.
long: Asymptotic series describe limiting behaviour without needing convergence. The coefficients are uniquely determined once the scale is fixed, even if the series diverges.
proof: Uniqueness follows by dividing successively by the scale functions and taking limits.
consequence: It formalises the divergent expansions ubiquitous in applied mathematics.

title: Jacobi Theta Functions and Modular Transformations
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: Theta functions are Gaussian Fourier series that transform under the modular inversion of their parameter with a square-root prefactor.
latex: \vartheta(z|\tau)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}e^{\pi i n^2\tau+2\pi i n z},\quad \vartheta(z/\tau|-1/\tau)=\sqrt{-i\tau}\,e^{\pi i z^2/\tau}\vartheta(z|\tau)
short: Poisson summation turns a theta series into a modular transform.
long: Poisson summation turns a theta series into a modular transform. Theta functions provide Fourier expansions of elliptic functions and heat-kernel traces on circles.
proof: Apply the Poisson summation formula to the Gaussian summands and complete the square in the Fourier variable.
consequence: It links elliptic functions, number theory, and conformal field theory.

title: Navier–Stokes Existence and Smoothness (Open)
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: For the three-dimensional incompressible Navier–Stokes equations with smooth initial data, global existence of smooth solutions is not known; weak solutions exist but their uniqueness and regularity remain open.
short: The fundamental regularity question for 3D fluid flow is unresolved.
long: The fundamental regularity question for 3D fluid flow is unresolved. Existence of finite-energy weak solutions was proved by Leray; the missing step is ruling out finite-time singularities.
proof: Open. Leray constructed global weak solutions via Galerkin approximations and energy estimates; whether they remain smooth is unknown, and the problem is one of the Clay Millennium Prize problems.
consequence: Resolution would transform the mathematical foundations of fluid mechanics.

title: The Second Isomorphism Theorem for Groups
subject: Abstract Algebra
statement: If H is a subgroup and N a normal subgroup of G, then HN is a subgroup, H∩N is normal in H, and HN/N is isomorphic to H/(H∩N).
short: Multiplying by a normal subgroup and then quotienting is the same as quotienting by the overlap.
long: Multiplying by a normal subgroup and then quotienting is the same as quotienting by the overlap. The natural map h ↦ hN from H onto HN/N is a homomorphism with kernel H∩N.
proof: Define φ(h)=hN; it is surjective onto HN/N and its kernel is H∩N, so the first isomorphism theorem gives the claim.
consequence: It is the standard tool for computing quotients of products and for normaliser calculations in finite group theory.

title: The Third Isomorphism Theorem for Groups
subject: Abstract Algebra
statement: If N and H are normal subgroups of G with N contained in H, then H/N is normal in G/N and (G/N)/(H/N) is isomorphic to G/H.
short: Quotienting twice is the same as quotienting once by the larger subgroup.
long: Quotienting twice is the same as quotienting once by the larger subgroup. The map gN ↦ gH is well defined precisely because N is contained in H.
proof: Define φ(gN)=gH; well-definedness follows from N⊆H, and ker φ=H/N, so apply the first isomorphism theorem.
consequence: It permits iterative quotient constructions and underlies the Jordan–Hölder programme for composition series.

title: The Correspondence Theorem for Subgroups
subject: Abstract Algebra
statement: For a normal subgroup N of G, subgroups of the quotient G/N correspond bijectively to subgroups of G containing N, preserving normality and indices.
short: Subgroups of a quotient are exactly the subgroups above the kernel, viewed from below.
long: Subgroups of a quotient are exactly the subgroups above the kernel, viewed from below. The correspondence sends K to K/N and its inverse sends L to its preimage under the quotient map.
proof: The quotient map q:G→G/N induces K↦q(K) and L↦q^{-1}(L); these are inverse because q^{-1}(q(K))=KN=K when N⊆K.
consequence: It reduces the subgroup lattice of a quotient to a segment of the original lattice.

title: The Sylow Theorems
subject: Abstract Algebra
statement: For a finite group of order p^n m with p not dividing m, Sylow p-subgroups exist, are conjugate, and their number is congruent to 1 modulo p and divides m.
short: The prime-power part of a finite group's order controls a rich family of conjugate subgroups.
long: The prime-power part of a finite group's order controls a rich family of conjugate subgroups. The three Sylow theorems give existence of maximal p-subgroups, conjugacy of all of them, and arithmetic restrictions on their count.
proof: Existence follows by induction on group order using the class equation; conjugacy follows from the orbit–stabiliser theorem acting on Sylow subgroups; the congruences come from counting those orbits.
consequence: They give the main structural classification of finite groups of small order and prove many groups are not simple.

title: Cauchy's Theorem for Finite Groups
subject: Abstract Algebra
statement: If a prime p divides the order of a finite group G, then G contains an element of order p.
short: Every prime dividing a group's order appears as the order of an actual element.
long: Every prime dividing a group's order appears as the order of an actual element. The standard proof counts tuples (g_1,...,g_p) with product 1, using a cyclic group action.
proof: Let X be the set of p-tuples with product 1 and let the cyclic group of order p rotate entries; fixed points are constant tuples, so |X| and the number of fixed points are congruent mod p, forcing a nonidentity element of order p.
consequence: It is the first major partial converse to Lagrange's theorem and a key ingredient in the Sylow theorems.

title: The Class Equation of a Finite Group
subject: Abstract Algebra
statement: The order of a finite group equals the size of its centre plus the sum of the indices of the centralisers of representatives of the noncentral conjugacy classes.
short: A group splits into its centre and the conjugacy classes of its noncentral elements.
long: A group splits into its centre and the conjugacy classes of its noncentral elements. Conjugacy classes partition G, and the class of x has size [G:C_G(x)] by the orbit–stabiliser theorem.
proof: Partition G into conjugacy classes; a class has size one exactly for central elements, and the other sizes are the centraliser indices.
consequence: It proves that every finite p-group has a nontrivial centre and underlies Sylow's existence proof.

title: Solvable Groups and the Derived Series
subject: Abstract Algebra
statement: A group is solvable if its derived series G ⊇ G' ⊇ G'' ⊇ ... reaches the trivial subgroup after finitely many steps.
short: Solvability measures how far a group is from being abelian, in finitely many commutator steps.
long: Solvability measures how far a group is from being abelian, in finitely many commutator steps. Equivalently a group has a subnormal series with abelian factor groups.
proof: The equivalence follows because a subgroup with abelian quotient contains the corresponding derived subgroup.
consequence: Solvable groups are precisely the Galois groups of polynomials solvable by radicals.

title: Nilpotent Groups and the Lower Central Series
subject: Abstract Algebra
statement: A group is nilpotent if its lower central series G ⊇ [G,G] ⊇ [[G,G],G] ⊇ ... terminates at the trivial subgroup.
short: Nilpotent groups are close to abelian in a stronger, central sense than solvable groups.
long: Nilpotent groups are close to abelian in a stronger, central sense than solvable groups. Every nilpotent group is solvable, but the converse fails, as the symmetric group S_3 shows.
proof: Each quotient γ_n/γ_{n+1} is abelian, giving a subnormal series with abelian factors, hence solvability.
consequence: Finite nilpotent groups are direct products of their Sylow subgroups, which makes their structure transparent.

title: The Quaternion Group as a Nonabelian Group of Order Eight
subject: Abstract Algebra
statement: The quaternion group Q_8 = {±1, ±i, ±j, ±k} with i²=j²=k²=ijk=−1 is a nonabelian group of order eight in which every subgroup is normal.
short: A tiny group where i times j is the negative of j times i.
long: A tiny group where i times j is the negative of j times i. It is the smallest example of a Hamiltonian group: a nonabelian group all of whose subgroups are normal.
proof: Direct multiplication of the eight symbols verifies the group axioms; ij=−ji gives noncommutativity, and every subgroup is either central or of index two, hence normal.
consequence: It shows that being a group with all subgroups normal does not force commutativity.

title: The Dihedral Groups and Symmetries of a Polygon
subject: Abstract Algebra
statement: The dihedral group D_n is generated by a rotation r of order n and a reflection s with srs = r^{-1}, and has order 2n.
short: Dihedral groups are the symmetry groups of regular polygons.
long: Dihedral groups are the symmetry groups of regular polygons. The relations encode that reflecting conjugates a rotation into its inverse.
proof: Every symmetry is a power of r followed by at most one reflection, giving 2n distinct elements, and the stated relations determine all products.
consequence: Dihedral groups are the standard source of small finite groups and appear throughout crystallography.

title: Simplicity of the Alternating Group A_n for n at Least Five
subject: Abstract Algebra
statement: For n ≥ 5 the alternating group A_n has no nontrivial proper normal subgroup.
short: Beyond degree four the even permutations form a simple group.
long: Beyond degree four the even permutations form a simple group. The proof uses that A_n is generated by 3-cycles and that any nontrivial normal subgroup contains a 3-cycle.
proof: Conjugating a nonidentity element and using commutators with 3-cycles produces a 3-cycle inside any nontrivial normal subgroup; since all 3-cycles are conjugate in A_n for n≥5, the subgroup is all of A_n.
consequence: This simplicity is the starting point of the classification of finite simple groups and explains the unsolvability of the general quintic.
